children: The Royal Government of Bhutan has moved approximately 400 Bitcoin, worth around $30.62 million, to an unidentified external address, according to blockchain analytics firm Lookonchain. The transfer leaves Bhutan's remaining labeled on-chain holdings at roughly 518 BTC, a fraction of what the country controlled less than two years ago.

For context on how dramatic that decline is: Bhutan's tracked Bitcoin holdings peaked at around 13,000 BTC in October 2024. Today's 518 BTC represents a reduction of roughly 96% from that high-water mark.

The transfers are attributed primarily to Druk Holding and Investments, the country's sovereign wealth fund, which has been steadily routing Bitcoin to a variety of counterparties throughout 2026. Recipients have included Binance, Galaxy Digital, and QCP Capital, among others. In June alone, 533 BTC moved to Binance in a single transaction.

The pattern is consistent: transactions in the 300 to 500 BTC range, sent to a mix of exchanges and institutional trading desks, with cumulative outflows from Bhutan's labeled wallets exceeding hundreds of millions of dollars this year.

The most recent 400 BTC transfer, however, went to an unlabeled address. That distinction matters. When coins move to a named exchange, analysts can at least infer intent. An unlabeled destination offers nothing, which is exactly why it tends to produce more speculation than certainty.

Bhutan built its Bitcoin position through state-backed hydropower mining that began in 2019. The country's rivers and mountain terrain gave it access to cheap, renewable electricity at scale, and the government quietly accumulated Bitcoin long before most sovereign observers knew it was in the game.

Official commentary from Bhutan has historically been cautious. Past statements from government representatives have framed transfers as liquidity management rather than outright sales, suggesting the kingdom views its Bitcoin holdings more like a treasury instrument than a static reserve.
Mining inflows to Bhutan's labeled wallets have been minimal for more than a year, meaning the outflows aren't being replenished at anything close to the pace they're leaving.

One concrete data point that adds texture: in December 2025, Bhutan pledged up to 10,000 BTC toward the development of the Gelephu Mindfulness City project, an ambitious new urban development initiative. If that pledge was honored through actual Bitcoin transfers rather than a paper allocation, it would account for a substantial portion of the decline in labeled holdings. Whether those coins moved to a development fund, were sold to raise fiat for construction, or are sitting in wallets that simply haven't been labeled yet is unclear from on-chain data alone.

The kingdom is a small country with a population of roughly 700,000 people. At peak holdings, the value of 13,000 BTC relative to Bhutan's GDP would have been extraordinary for any nation, let alone one with the economic footprint of a mid-sized city.

Bhutan's cumulative 2026 outflows, measured in the hundreds of millions of dollars, represent real potential sell pressure regardless of the ultimate destination. If even a portion of those coins hit spot markets, the volume is meaningful at a market structure level.

El Salvador, which made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021, has also periodically moved coins in ways that attracted scrutiny. The United States holds a large amount of Bitcoin seized through law enforcement actions. Any of these holders making large, opaque transfers tends to rattle the market's confidence in the stability of sovereign-level supply.

title: Bhutan transfers 400 BTC to unlabelled address, leaving sovereign holdings at 518 BTC
